opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, Xiaojun, it's great to be here.

I think this question goes to the heart of what separates an embodied-intelligence company from a traditional robotics or automation company.

Look at the classic industrial robot business. For each new task, a station on an assembly line or a particular part to pick, you send engineers to the site. They do the fixturing, calibrate the cameras, write task-specific code, and tune it for weeks. It works, but it's essentially a project business. Your marginal cost per deployment barely falls, because every new scene is a new engineering job. That kind of business can be profitable, but it doesn't scale the way people imagine when they talk about embodied intelligence changing the world.

Generalization changes the economics. If one model can handle a new object, a new shelf layout, new lighting, a new store, without someone rewriting the system, then the cost of each additional deployment drops sharply. You go from selling engineering hours to selling a product. That's the difference between a services company and a platform company, and it's why generalization isn't just a technical nice-to-have. It's what makes the business model possible at all.

There's also a flywheel. Without generalization, every deployment is an island. The data you collect in one factory doesn't help much in another, because the solution was hand-crafted for that environment. With a generalizable model, every robot in the field becomes a data source that improves the shared model, and the better model opens up more scenarios. The value compounds instead of resetting with each customer.

I want to be realistic, though. Generalization isn't binary, and we're not at the point where you can drop a humanoid into any home and have it do anything. So in practice the strategy is to find verticals, like retail, pharmacies, or certain logistics and manufacturing tasks, where the required generalization is achievable now. Within that domain, the robot should handle the long tail of variation, tens of thousands of different products and changing layouts, without per-site engineering. That's a commercially meaningful level of generalization. Then you expand the boundary step by step.

And data is the bottleneck. For a long time the field was stuck because real-world robot data is so expensive to collect. That's why I've put so much emphasis on synthetic data and simulation: generating huge amounts of diverse training data so the model sees variation it would never encounter in a few real deployments. Combined with a smaller amount of real data, that's what gets you to generalization at a cost that makes sense.

So to sum up: without generalization, you're a custom automation shop. With it, you can become a product company with real scaling economics and a data flywheel. For anyone trying to build a large embodied-intelligence company, I think that's the central question.

r001.rationale: The response says each new scene requires a new engineering job and that marginal deployment costs barely fall.

r002.rationale: It describes sending engineers to each site for task-specific setup and explains that this project-based labor limits scaling.

fable-5.1.text:
Because without generalization, embodied intelligence isn't really a product company, it's a project company. Think about what happens if your robot's capability doesn't transfer: every time a customer brings you a new scene, a new object, a new task, you have to send engineers on site, collect data again, tune again, re-deploy. Each customer becomes a bespoke integration. That's the traditional system-integrator business, and it's been around for decades in industrial automation. The margins are thin, it scales linearly with headcount, and it doesn't compound.

What a true embodied-intelligence company sells is a model, a brain, that works across environments it hasn't seen before. The whole economic logic of AI is that you invest heavily in training once, and then deployment becomes nearly zero-marginal-cost. That logic only holds if the model generalizes. If it doesn't, you've just built a very expensive way of doing what integrators already do.

And there's a deeper point. Generalization is what lets the data flywheel actually turn. When a robot can go into a new household or a new factory and perform reasonably well out of the box, you can deploy at scale, collect real-world data from thousands of sites, and that data improves the next model, which generalizes better, which lets you deploy even wider. Without the initial generalization, you never get the deployment scale, and without scale, you never get the data. You're stuck collecting in your own lab, which is slow and expensive and never covers the long tail.

So when I look at this field, I'd say generalization isn't one feature among many. It's the thing that decides whether you have a business model at all, or just a sequence of demos.

r001.rationale: It says each new scene requires on-site engineering, fresh data collection, tuning, and redeployment, while generalization is what allows deployment to approach zero marginal cost.

r002.rationale: It describes sending engineers for each bespoke integration and says this project-style business scales linearly with headcount.

astra-6.text:
Because the business ultimately depends on whether you can reuse what the robot has learned. If every new customer, every new environment, and every new task requires you to collect a separate dataset and do a lot of custom engineering, then each deployment becomes another project. You may generate revenue, but your costs grow along with it.

Generalization is what can change that economics. A robot needs to handle differences in objects, layouts, and conditions without us having to anticipate and program every variation. Then the capabilities we build for one deployment can help with the next, and the cost of delivering useful work can come down.

That doesn’t mean you need a robot that can do everything from day one. You can start with a narrow application. But even within that application, the real world keeps changing. So generalization isn’t just a research benchmark—it’s central to whether the company can scale.

r001.rationale: It says each new customer, environment, or task may require a separate dataset and custom engineering, making costs grow with deployments rather than fall.

r002.rationale: It links repeated custom engineering for each deployment to growing costs and says generalization is central to whether the company can scale.

sol-6.1.text:
Because if every new task or every new customer site requires us to collect a new dataset, retrain the model, and send engineers to make it work, then we’re essentially running a custom integration business. We can charge for each project, but our costs grow with the number of deployments. It’s very difficult to scale that into a broadly useful robotics company.

Generalization changes that economics. The robot needs to take capabilities it has learned and apply them to new objects, new environments, and variations of a task without starting from scratch. That means the same underlying system can serve more customers, while the cost and time required for each deployment come down.

Of course, it doesn’t have to do everything on day one. You can start with a bounded set of applications. But even within that scope, the real world keeps changing. If the robot only works under the exact conditions you trained it on, you haven’t really solved the customer’s problem. So generalization is both a technical requirement for reliability and the foundation for a scalable business model.

r001.rationale: The response says each new task or customer site can require a new dataset and retraining, making costs grow with deployments rather than fall.

r002.rationale: It says engineers may need to be sent to make each deployment work, turning the business into custom integration that is difficult to scale.
